newsitem.title: MEXICO: Televisa to present rebound strategy in New York.
newsitem.headline: Televisa to present rebound strategy in New York.

text.p: Mexican media firm Grupo Televisa SA will have to stage an outstanding show on Wednesday when it presents its much-ballyhooed Televisa 2000 strategy plan to shareholders and analysts in New York.

The media giant faces an uphill battle convincing skeptics it can rebound following the recent death of its charismatic chairman Emilio Azcarraga Milmo and the steady loss of market share to its hungry rival TV Azteca, analysts said on Tuesday.
"They will have to pull some rabbits out of a hat to meet the expectations built up for this plan," a Mexico City industry analyst told Reuters.
Early this year, Televisa began talking about unveiling a long-term strategic plan to claw back its lost market share and deepen cost-cutting efforts undertaken after the 1995 peso crisis.
The plan took on a greater sense of urgency and importance in financial markets following the death of Azcarraga Milmo in April and the subsequent rise to power of his son Emilio Azcarraga Jean, 29.

Despite the creation of a new executive committee to broaden decision making at the family-run company, the new chief executive's young age left some analysts wondering if the company had been left in capable hands. Investors reacted negatively as well, driving down the stock price.

"A lot of people trusted Emilio Azcarraga Milmo. He had a vision....now, you can buy the idea they'll make it without him or be skeptical," said Francisco Rivero, an analyst at Valores Finamex in New York.
Analysts said the plan will highlight a combination of cost-cutting moves, new programming, and news on its satellite TV venture with News Corp. It will also outline the executive committee's role.

Mexican newspaper Reforma on Tuesday said the plan will focus on cutting administrative costs by 35 percent within the next few years, mostly by reducing the number of top executives and cutting salaries.
Quoting unnamed company officials, Reforma said Televisa will also announce it has scrapped plans to sell some of its units, including cable television outfit Cablevision.
The company may not need extra cash following the $650 million it received last week for the sale of its stake in PanAmSat Corp., analysts said.
Televisa officials on Tuesday were unavailable for comment on the report.
Analysts said they would welcome any cost-cutting moves, but sounded a note of caution by pointing out that Televisa never fully carried out past promises to trim fat.
And some agreed they would rather hear more news about new programming to boost market share and ad revenues than cost-cutting.
"With a media company you can have huge costs, but if your top line's going throught the roof, who cares about the costs?" the Mexico City analyst said.

Rivero said he thought Televisa had begun to turn the tide on its rating loss in the first quarter. He said Televisa's four national channels lost about 50 basis points to TV Azteca in that period -- much below the average quarterly loss in market share last year of about 150 basis points.
